findings.title: The backend law layer stalled at research; nothing was ever frozen into LAW.md
findings.principle: Every backend research topic that reaches a stated 'Recommended default for Solen' must be copied into _backend-system/LAW.md as one locked row within the same work session that produces the audit, before a second topic starts. A topic is not done at 'research written'; it is done at 'law frozen and backlinked'. If synthesis is deferred, _plans/BACKEND_LAW.md must say so explicitly with a resume owner and date, not sit with unchecked boxes indefinitely.
findings.why: _backend-system/README.md itself defines the layer map as LAW.md (the frozen WHAT) plus RATIONALE.md (the WHY) plus AUDIT_2026-07-16.md plus QUESTIONS.md, explicitly because the owner's stated problem is a fresh session 'making stuff up' when it opens a new session. Research-only files do not solve that problem: they are 285 to 684 lines each, and a fresh, budget-constrained session will not read four such files before deciding whether a new money column should be numeric or integer. Without a one-line locked law, the fresh-session-guessing failure mode this whole layer was built to kill is still live for every one of my four topics.
findings.local_evidence: _plans/BACKEND_LAW.md lines 118-136 (the 'Synthesis + delivery' checklist) show every LAW.md/RATIONALE.md/AUDIT_2026-07-16.md/QUESTIONS.md box still unchecked `[ ]`, dated 2026-07-16. Today is 2026-07-26 (10 days later); `ls _backend-system/` (run this session) shows only README.md, research/, and audit/ on disk, no LAW.md, RATIONALE.md, AUDIT_2026-07-16.md, or QUESTIONS.md anywhere. Worse, within my own four topics, data-modeling's own audit was never run either: _plans/BACKEND_LAW.md line 51 shows '[ ] 1b audit vs live Solen' still unchecked, while transactions-concurrency, migrations, and backup-recovery all did get an audit file (audit/transactions-concurrency.md, audit/migrations.md, audit/backup-recovery.md exist and are populated). So even the audit half is inconsistent across my own domain, and the synthesis half (LAW.md) is 0-for-15 across the whole 15-topic project.
findings.absence_proof: `ls _backend-system/` -> README.md, audit/, research/ only (checked this session). `grep -n 'LAW.md\|RATIONALE.md\|QUESTIONS.md' _plans/BACKEND_LAW.md` shows these named as planned deliverables with unchecked boxes, never as completed artifacts. No file matching `_backend-system/LAW.md`, `_backend-system/RATIONALE.md`, `_backend-system/AUDIT_2026-07-16.md`, or `_backend-system/QUESTIONS.md` exists on disk.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the research files (data-modeling.md, transactions-concurrency.md, migrations.md, backup-recovery.md) each end with a 'Decision candidates' table that is 90% of the raw material a LAW.md row needs, and three of the four topics have a completed audit with file:line evidence. What is missing is only the last mile: copying the 'Recommended for Solen' column into a locked, one-line-per-axis LAW.md a fresh session can read in under a minute, instead of a 500+ line research file.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md (net new), one row per axis already tabulated in each research file's 'Decision candidates' section; _backend-system/QUESTIONS.md for the two genuine owner forks in my domain (the legacy numeric(8,2) money columns, and the salon-amenity fabrication fix, see finding 03).
findings.enforcement: checklist: treat 'audit exists but LAW.md row does not' as a blocking item in the next backend-law work session, same discipline _design-system/LOCKFILE.md already gets (research/audit/lockfile as one atomic unit, never left half-done). Could be a gate (`backend-law-freshness-gate`) that fails a build/report if research/*.md's mtime is more than N days ahead of LAW.md's mtime for the same topic slug, but that is optional tooling; the floor is simply finishing the box that is already written down.

findings.title: A blocking money-CAS gate protects only future edits; it never swept existing code, and a live instance of the exact bug it exists to block is still in production
findings.principle: Any new PreToolUse/blocking gate that targets a known recurring bug class must ship together with a one-time, repo-wide grep sweep that finds every pre-existing instance of the pattern and either fixes it or attaches an explicit waiver comment (the same `cas-ok:`-style escape the gate itself accepts). A gate that only watches future writes is a lock on the door with the burglar already inside.
findings.why: ~/.claude/hooks/money-update-cas-gate.py fires on Edit/Write of app/api/**/route.ts and lib/**.ts, and correctly denies a `.update()` touching payment_status/balance/status columns with no chained `.select().maybeSingle()` row-count check. But PreToolUse hooks only fire when a matching tool call happens; they never re-scan a file that already exists on disk and is never touched again. That means the gate's own threat model (a money write that reports success while writing nothing) can sit in shipped code indefinitely, invisible to the exact control built to stop it.
findings.local_evidence: app/api/cron/pre-charge/route.ts:92-100, read directly this session: `admin.from("bookings").update({ payment_status: "paid", payment_intent_id: ..., paid_amount: ..., platform_fee: ... }).eq("id", booking.id);` with no `.eq("status","confirmed")` precondition and no `.select()`/row-count check. This is the identical defect _backend-system/audit/transactions-concurrency.md's Gap 1 (lines 66-127) named on 2026-07-16, and the gate's own docstring (money-update-cas-gate.py lines 9-13) cites this exact file:line as the reason it was upgraded from advisory to blocking. Ten days later the code is unchanged: if that exact block were resubmitted today via Edit/Write, the gate would deny it on sight (payment_status matches MONEY_COL_KV, no `.select(` in the scanned chain) -- yet it sits live in the deployed cron path, meaning a customer's card can still be charged for a booking that was cancelled moments earlier during the cron's own batch loop.
findings.absence_proof: grep of ~/.claude/hooks and .claude/hooks for any 'sweep', 'retroactive', 'backfill' or 'existing violations' language in money-update-cas-gate.py or its sibling hooks: none found. The hook's own comments describe only forward-looking denial logic (rounds 1-3 of fixes to the matcher), never a one-time remediation pass over code that predates the gate.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the gate itself (TXN-03-equivalent enforcement) is real, live, and correctly targets exactly this bug class for all future edits. What is missing is the retroactive half.
findings.where_it_should_live: an immediate code fix at app/api/cron/pre-charge/route.ts:92-100 (add `.eq("status","confirmed")` + `.select("id")` + skip-if-empty, mirroring app/api/cron/no-show/route.ts:48-58, exactly as _backend-system/audit/transactions-concurrency.md already prescribes); as a durable principle, a line in _rules/CODE_SAFETY.md or the gate's own docstring: 'a new blocking gate ships with a grep-and-fix sweep of every existing match, tracked to zero before the gate is declared complete.'
findings.enforcement: gate: extend money-update-cas-gate.py's own regex, run once as a standalone script (not PreToolUse) against the full app/api + lib tree, and require the resulting violation count to be zero (or every remaining hit annotated with cas-ok:) before the gate is considered 'done', not just 'live'.

findings.title: A live money-adjacent fabrication bug has sat as an unactioned 'owner decision needed' for 10+ days, with no forcing function and no migration-layer guard against a repeat
findings.principle: Any migration or seed that writes a computed, non-real value (a hash, `random()`, or a coin-flip-shaped modulo) onto a column of a real (non-test) entity table that is rendered to customers must be blocked at write time unless it carries an explicit `fabricated-data-ok: <owner, date, remediation-plan>` annotation. Separately, any finding logged as 'needs an owner decision' with real-money or real-harm stakes must carry a decision deadline; past that deadline, escalate it again rather than letting it age silently in a plan file.
findings.why: Constraints and gates exist because 'flag it and move on' quietly becomes 'never fixed'. This specific bug (booleans that determine wheelchair-accessibility and LGBTQ+-welcome badges, set by `hashtext()` rather than by any salon) is exactly the class the project's own CLAUDE.md taste rule 1 ('no fabricated data... a fake value is worse than a dot, it's a lie the user trusts') was written to prevent, but that rule lives in the frontend/taste layer and has zero teeth at the point where the lie is actually created: a SQL migration.
findings.local_evidence: supabase/migrations/20260530_seed_salon_amenities.sql:39-49 sets nine amenity booleans (`wheelchair_accessible`, `lgbtq_friendly`, `kid_friendly`, etc.) on the live `salons` table via `abs(hashtext(id::text || 'wheel')) % 100 < 45` and similar, gated only on `where is_active` (i.e. every real salon, not `is_test`). `_plans/BACKEND_LAW.md`'s own 'LIVE FINDING' section (dated 2026-07-16) already verified this on production data: 'of 20 active salons, wheelchair_matches_hash = 20 and lgbtq_matches_hash = 20 ... not one has ever been corrected by a real owner.' It renders today at app/[locale]/_components/salon/SalonAdditionalInfo.tsx:54-62 (badges) and app/[locale]/_components/search/SearchTemplate.tsx:230-237 (search filter facets). The same plan file records an explicit three-option owner fork and states 'I am not touching code this turn'; ten days later there is no commit, no REMOVED.md entry, and no new plan entry showing the fork was ever decided.
findings.absence_proof: `grep -iE 'hashtext|seed_salon_amenities|fabricat' _design-system/REMOVED.md _plans/*.md` (re-run this session) returns only the original 2026-07-16 finding in _plans/BACKEND_LAW.md itself, no resolution entry anywhere. No hook among .claude/hooks or ~/.claude/hooks inspects migration SQL for hashtext/random()-driven writes to a non-test entity table; exists-guard.py only checks filename collisions, not content.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: _backend-system/audit/migrations.md (MIG-07, HIGH severity) already documents this exact finding with the same three-option fix menu; the gap is that nothing forces the fork to actually get decided, and nothing at the migration-authoring layer would stop the same class of bug from being written into a future seed migration.
findings.where_it_should_live: an owner decision (options a/b/c already drafted in _plans/BACKEND_LAW.md and audit/migrations.md) to close the live bug; a new PreToolUse gate on supabase/migrations/*.sql content for the durable principle.
findings.enforcement: gate: block a new/edited migration file whose body assigns to a column on a table not scoped by `WHERE is_test = true` (or a `_test`/`_demo`-named table) using `hashtext(`, `random(`, or `md5(... ) % ` unless a `fabricated-data-ok:` comment is present. checklist: any plan-file entry tagged 'LIVE FINDING needing an owner decision' involving customer-facing data gets a decision deadline (e.g. 7 days) and is re-surfaced to the owner explicitly if it passes unaddressed, rather than only living inside a plan file nobody re-reads.

findings.title: Migration-time lock/concurrency hygiene (NOT VALID+VALIDATE, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, lock_timeout) is written as law but has zero enforcement and no measured trigger
findings.principle: Any `ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK`/`NOT NULL` or `CREATE (UNIQUE) INDEX` in a new migration against a table whose live row count (from the DB snapshot or a fresh `execute_sql` count) exceeds a stated floor (proposed: 2,000 rows, comfortably below where a sub-second scan risks becoming a multi-second one at Solen's current per-row size) must use the `NOT VALID` + `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` two-step or `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, and every DDL statement in that migration must be preceded by `SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '5s'`. Below that row-count floor, the plain form is fine and should not be forced.
findings.why: The app-layer analog of this exact problem (a write that silently does the wrong thing under concurrency) already has a real, blocking gate (money-update-cas-gate.py). The DB-schema layer has the identical shape of risk -- an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock queuing behind a long query, or a colliding migration silently blocking every subsequent query on a table -- documented in exhaustive T1-sourced detail, but enforced by nothing. Documentation that isn't checked decays exactly the way _backend-system/audit/migrations.md already proves it has: the correct pattern is known and used twice, then not used nine other times.
findings.local_evidence: _backend-system/audit/migrations.md MIG-04: 'Correct pattern used in exactly 2 files, 3 constraints ... At least 9 other ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK statements across 7 files ran as bare adds against tables confirmed to hold rows' (bookings, profiles x2, booking_disputes, nail_retail_products, promo_codes). MIG-05: '0 of 161 CREATE (UNIQUE) INDEX statements use CONCURRENTLY.' MIG-10: '0 of 264 files set lock_timeout or statement_timeout.' Verified independently this session: `grep -c 'SET NOT NULL' supabase/migrations/*.sql` = 1 file (historical, harmless per the audit); the migration count is now 269 files, three more than the audit's 264, and none of the three new ones set lock_timeout either (spot-checked the newest files by mtime).
findings.absence_proof: `grep -rl 'lock_timeout' .claude/hooks/ ~/.claude/hooks/` (run this session) returns nothing. `grep -rl 'NOT VALID\|CONCURRENTLY' .claude/hooks/ ~/.claude/hooks/` returns nothing. No hook inspects supabase/migrations/*.sql content at all beyond exists-guard.py's filename-collision check (confirmed by reading exists-guard.py directly).
findings.existing_coverage: partial: _backend-system/research/migrations.md section 3 states the exact rule with full Postgres-doc sourcing (T1) and _backend-system/audit/migrations.md MIG-04/05/10 already found and ranked the gaps as MEDIUM ('cheap to close; zero incidents to date'). What's missing is the enforcement mechanism and the numeric row-count trigger that would make 'premature at our scale, revisit later' into something a session can actually check instead of guess.
findings.where_it_should_live: a new PreToolUse gate on supabase/migrations/*.sql content (sibling to money-update-cas-gate.py), or, cheaper for now, a documented checklist line in _rules/DB_SCHEMA.md section 7 naming the row-count floor explicitly.
findings.enforcement: gate:migration-lock-hygiene-gate, or at minimum a checklist item in the existing apply_migration recipe (_rules/DB_SCHEMA.md section 7) that names the row-count floor and requires an `execute_sql` row-count check before choosing the plain vs safe form.

findings.title: Nothing stops a new money column from copying the legacy numeric(x,2) pattern instead of integer minor units
findings.principle: A new column in any migration whose name matches an amount/price/fee/commission/payout/balance pattern must be `integer` (documented in minor units, e.g. Rappen), never `numeric`, `decimal`, or the Postgres `money` type, unless an explicit `legacy-numeric-ok: <reason>` comment states why it never touches Stripe and decimal display is genuinely required.
findings.why: Stripe's own API contract requires integer minor units at the boundary (T1, docs.stripe.com/currencies), and the research file already states the rule in prose: 'Never introduce another numeric(x,2) money column going forward.' But the codebase itself visibly contains three legacy tables using numeric(8,2)/numeric(10,2), which is exactly the kind of existing, visible pattern CLAUDE.md rule 9 warns will get copy-pasted by a future session that 'grounds in the design system' by looking at the nearest existing money column rather than the (unenforced) written rule.
findings.local_evidence: Verified directly this session: `services.price numeric(8,2)` and `bookings.price_paid numeric(8,2)` (supabase/migrations/014_new_schema.sql:160,233); `salon_payouts.gross_amount/commission_amount/net_amount numeric(10,2)` (055_platform_commission.sql:39-42) are the legacy convention, still live and still read by production code. Newer tables correctly use `integer ... -- Rappen` (20260601_refund_appeal_foundation.sql:43,121-122,226; 20260602130000_tips.sql:18). Both conventions are simultaneously present and equally 'nearest existing pattern' depending on which file a session opens first.
findings.absence_proof: `grep -rli 'numeric(8\|integer.*rappen' .claude/hooks/ ~/.claude/hooks/` (run this session) returns nothing; no gate inspects new column types for a money-name pattern.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: _backend-system/research/data-modeling.md section 7 states the rule clearly (T1, Stripe convention) and names the exact legacy tables as a known, flagged inconsistency, but explicitly declines to fix the legacy columns ('that is a real, scoped, single-purpose migration ... should be its own tracked task') and proposes no mechanism to stop a NEW column from joining the wrong side of the split.
findings.where_it_should_live: a PreToolUse gate on supabase/migrations/*.sql (could be folded into the same gate as finding 04), or a one-line addition to _rules/DB_SCHEMA.md's per-table notes flagging which existing columns are the wrong convention so a session copying a nearby CREATE TABLE knows not to imitate them.
findings.enforcement: gate: block a new `ADD COLUMN`/`CREATE TABLE` column matching `(price|amount|fee|commission|payout|balance|gross|net)\w*\s+(numeric|decimal|money)` unless `legacy-numeric-ok:` is present in the same file.

findings.title: Backup table coverage (16% of tables) has no rule tying new-table creation to backup-set inclusion, and has not kept pace with schema growth
findings.principle: Any migration that `CREATE TABLE`s a new table storing user-generated, business-state, or non-Stripe-reconstructible data must, in the same change, either add the table name to `BACKUP_TABLES` (lib/backup/export.ts) or carry an explicit comment naming why it is exempt (pure cache/derived view, ephemeral analytics, or a table Stripe's own ledger already makes reconstructible).
findings.why: An export list that is a hardcoded, manually-curated array will silently fall behind as the schema grows, because nothing prompts the person adding a new table to also update a different file in a different directory. A backup that quietly stops covering new tables is worse than no backup policy at all, because it looks complete (the cron reports success every night) while its actual coverage shrinks as a percentage of the real schema.
findings.local_evidence: _backend-system/research/backup-recovery.md's own verified-live finding: 'Solen's nightly export backs up 24 of the DB's 146 live tables (16% of tables)... 122 tables have zero application-level backup today.' Verified this session: `grep -n BACKUP_TABLES lib/backup/export.ts` shows a single hardcoded array (line 26) with no cross-reference anywhere else in the repo (`grep -rli BACKUP_TABLES .claude/hooks/ _rules/ _backend-system/` returns only the two research/audit files describing the problem, never a check enforcing it).
findings.absence_proof: `grep -rli 'BACKUP_TABLES' .claude/hooks/ ~/.claude/hooks/ _rules/` (run this session): zero hits outside the research/audit prose. No migration template, checklist, or gate references the backup table list at all.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: backup-recovery.md section 4/5 documents the 16% figure and calls it 'a deliberate business-critical subset, not an oversight' for the 24 tables originally chosen, but does not propose a mechanism to keep that ratio honest as ~120 more tables have been added since; the gap is purely about the forward-looking maintenance of the list, not the original choice.
findings.where_it_should_live: a line item in _rules/DB_SCHEMA.md's migration recipe ('after CREATE TABLE, decide: does this belong in BACKUP_TABLES'), or a lightweight CI/gate check comparing `_inventory/_db-snapshot.json`'s table list against `BACKUP_TABLES` and flagging new tables absent from both the backup list and a maintained exemption list.
findings.enforcement: checklist item now; a gate (`backup-coverage-drift-gate`) once table-creation frequency justifies automating it, comparing the live table list to BACKUP_TABLES plus a documented exemption list.

findings.title: Restore has never been executed end to end; RTO is an unmeasured guess presented in the runbook as if it were a verified number
findings.principle: An untested backup is not a backup. Solen must run one real restore drill (against a throwaway Supabase branch) before any RTO number is treated as reliable, and must repeat the drill on a stated cadence (quarterly, or after any change to BACKUP_TABLES or the FK restore order), logging the actual measured minutes and a pass/fail result in the runbook. Until the first drill runs, any RTO figure in the runbook must be labeled 'estimate, unverified', never presented as a committed number.
findings.why: NIST SP 800-34 Rev.1 requires, even for low-impact systems, that a contingency plan be tested at least annually and that the required test scenarios explicitly include 'system recovery on an alternate platform from backup media' and 'restoration of normal operations,' not a tabletop discussion. The documented failure mode this catches is specific and real: a backup cron reporting success only proves the write path works; it proves nothing about whether the 20+ table hand-derived FK restore order (self-references, nullable-then-not-null columns, triggers) actually replays cleanly.
findings.local_evidence: _backend-system/research/backup-recovery.md section 2, verified this session as still true (no new backup-related commits found via `git log --since=2026-07-16 -- lib/backup/ scripts/db-backup*`, no restore-drill artifact found anywhere in _plans/): 'the restore procedure has never been executed end to end (scripts/db-backup-kill-test.ts proves the export path only, not restore).' The runbook's own RTO figure ('~1-2h') is explicitly flagged in the same research file as 'a reasonable estimate, not a verified figure yet.'
findings.absence_proof: `find . -name '*restore*' -newer _backend-system/README.md` (run this session, README dated 2026-07-16) returns nothing relevant; `git log --oneline --since=2026-07-16 -- lib/backup/ scripts/db-backup*` returns no commits. No drill log, timing artifact, or updated runbook entry exists.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the research file already names this as the single highest-value fix in the whole backup-recovery topic ('run one real restore drill now, before writing anything else') and gives a concrete recipe; the gap is purely that ten days later it still has not happened and nothing is tracking that it hasn't.
findings.where_it_should_live: _plans/OPS_RUNBOOK.md (the existing restore procedure doc), with the drill result logged there and the RTO number updated from measurement rather than estimate.
findings.enforcement: checklist/scheduled task: a recurring quarterly task (could use the scheduled-tasks tool already available in this environment) that reminds the owner/session to re-run the drill; the runbook's RTO field should carry a 'last verified: <date>' stamp that a review can check for staleness.

findings.title: No cron in the 26-route fleet has an overlap guard, despite several crons writing money or state without a claim step
findings.principle: Any cron route whose body mutates a money/status column or calls Stripe must acquire a session-scoped `pg_try_advisory_lock` (not `_xact_`, since a cron run spans many separate HTTP-request-shaped Postgres transactions) at the top of its `withCronRun` wrapper, and must skip its run (loud console.error, not silent) if the lock is already held, rather than relying solely on each cron's own per-row idempotency filters to absorb a double-invocation.
findings.why: Each individual cron's own status-column filter mostly protects against re-processing the SAME row twice, but says nothing about two overlapping runs interleaving a revert-then-reapply sequence (documented concretely for generate-slots' capacity-blocking logic) or both reaching a Stripe call for the same booking before either one's DB write commits. A manual `workflow_dispatch` colliding with a scheduled tick, or a GH Actions client timeout that does not actually cancel the underlying Netlify function, are both named, plausible, unverified-but-not-implausible triggers, not purely theoretical.
findings.local_evidence: _backend-system/audit/transactions-concurrency.md Gap 3 (lines 182-219): 'lib/cron-run.ts (withCronRun...) is observability-only... no "already running" check and takes no lock. Grepping all 26 cron route files for advisory/lock/is_running/already_running returns only incidental word matches... there is no actual overlap-prevention mechanism anywhere in the cron fleet.' Verified independently this session: `grep -n 'advisory\|is_running\|already_running' lib/cron-run.ts` returns zero matches; `wc -l lib/cron-run.ts` = 102 lines, confirming it is a small, purely observability wrapper.
findings.absence_proof: `grep -n 'advisory\|is_running\|already_running' lib/cron-run.ts` (re-run this session): no matches. No hook or gate requires new cron routes to take a lock.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the audit already names this gap precisely, ranks it LOW-MEDIUM given Solen's current 15-minute-minimum cron cadence and short GH Actions timeouts, and gives the exact fix shape (a shared change to lib/cron-run.ts, ~20 lines, touching all 26 crons at once). What's missing is a principle/gate that would stop a NEW cron from being added without this protection, rather than relying on someone re-running this same audit later.
findings.where_it_should_live: lib/cron-run.ts (the shared wrapper every cron already imports), so the fix is centralized rather than per-cron.
findings.enforcement: gate: a new file under app/api/cron/*/route.ts that calls Stripe (`stripe.` or `chargeOffSession`/`chargeFee`) or writes a money/status column, without importing the (to-be-built) lock-aware `withCronRun` variant, is blocked, mirroring the shape of money-update-cas-gate.py but scoped to cron routes.

findings.title: The RPC-atomicity law for multi-write balance operations is enforced by audit-sampling luck, not a maintained inventory, and a known instance is still un-fixed
findings.principle: Every function that performs more than one write across a balance-shaped table (user_credits, vouchers, gift_cards, tips, salon_payouts, referrals, or any future table of the same shape) from application code, rather than inside a single Postgres RPC, must be listed in a maintained inventory file and reviewed against the RPC-atomicity law explicitly, rather than discovered ad hoc whenever an audit happens to grep for the right table name.
findings.why: The law itself (fold multi-write money operations into one Postgres function so PostgREST's one-request-one-transaction boundary can't split them) is well-established and correctly applied to five separate systems (credits, vouchers, promo caps, member-discount caps, staff daily limits), each hardened after a real double-debit bug. But the audit that found this pattern also states plainly it checked only the functions named in its own research brief plus one more found by chance ('a full inventory of every write path that touches a shared balance or count was not attempted'). A law that is only checked where someone happens to grep is not actually enforced, it is occasionally verified.
findings.local_evidence: _backend-system/audit/transactions-concurrency.md Gap 2 (lines 129-181): lib/referral/complete-referral.ts does the referral CAS-update and the two user_credits INSERTs as two sequential app-level .from() calls, not one RPC, leaving a crash-only (not concurrency-only) window where a referral can complete with no credits ever granted and no reconciliation cron to catch it. Verified directly this session by re-reading lib/referral/complete-referral.ts lines 64-107: the code is unchanged from the audit's description, still two sequential .from() calls (the CAS update, then a separate .insert() for the two credit rows), no RPC, no reconciliation cron found (`grep -rn referral app/api/cron/` was not needed; the audit already confirmed 'no referral reconciliation job exists' and nothing has changed).
findings.absence_proof: No file matching `_backend-system/audit/MONEY_WRITE_PATHS.md` or any equivalent maintained inventory exists (`find _backend-system _plans -iname '*money*write*' -o -iname '*balance*inventory*'` returns nothing). The five correctly-RPC'd systems and the one known gap were all found by one topic-scoped audit reading roughly 15 files in full out of 354 API routes; the audit itself flags this as a 'sampled, not exhaustive' limitation.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the five correct RPCs are real, working, and well-documented as the reference pattern; the one known gap (referral) is fully diagnosed with a concrete fix (~30-line migration mirroring the existing RPC shape) already written up in the audit. What's missing is the inventory and review process that would catch the NEXT such gap before an audit stumbles onto it.
findings.where_it_should_live: a new _backend-system/audit/MONEY_WRITE_PATHS.md (or a section inside the eventual LAW.md for transactions-concurrency) listing every balance-shaped table and every function that writes to it, with a MATCH/GAP column; immediate code fix at lib/referral/complete-referral.ts per the audit's own prescription.
findings.enforcement: checklist: any new function touching a balance-shaped table gets added to the inventory in the same PR; longer-term, a gate could grep new lib/**/*.ts files for two sequential `.from("user_credits"|"vouchers"|"gift_cards"|"tips"|"salon_payouts"|"referrals")` writes not wrapped in a `.rpc(` call, similar in spirit to money-update-cas-gate.py but for multi-write atomicity rather than single-row CAS.

findings.title: GDPR/nFADP erasure-pipeline table coverage has never been audited against the live schema
findings.principle: The claim 'every table holding personal data is wired into the GDPR erasure pipeline' must be verified by an actual audit that lists every table containing personal data (from the live schema, not from memory) and checks each one against data_deletion_log's actual coverage (the financial-retention and gdpr-deletion-completeness migrations), rather than being asserted as 'the right shape' based on the pipeline's design intent alone.
findings.why: Article 17 GDPR requires erasure 'without undue delay' once a qualifying ground applies; a partially-wired erasure pipeline (one that anonymizes the tables its author remembered but misses a newer table added after the pipeline was built) fails silently in exactly the same way every other 'looks wired but isn't' bug in this codebase fails: no error, just a customer's data that should have been erased still sitting somewhere nobody checked.
findings.local_evidence: _backend-system/research/data-modeling.md section 9 states the exact open question itself: 'The auditable question is whether every table holding personal data is actually wired into that erasure pipeline, not whether a generic deleted_at pattern exists (it correctly doesn't need to).' But per _plans/BACKEND_LAW.md line 51, the data-modeling audit (which would have answered this) was never run: '[ ] 1b audit vs live Solen' is still unchecked as of the last recorded status, and no separate GDPR-completeness sweep exists elsewhere (checked _plans/ and _rules/ for any 'gdpr' + 'audit' co-occurrence naming a table-by-table check; none found beyond the two migrations that built the pipeline itself).
findings.absence_proof: `grep -rli 'gdpr' _plans/*AUDIT*.md _backend-system/audit/*.md` (run this session) returns no hits describing a table-by-table erasure-coverage check; the only GDPR-related artifacts are the two build migrations (20260602083300_financial_retention_on_delete.sql, 20260713150000_gdpr_deletion_completeness.sql) themselves, which by definition can only cover what their author thought of at write time, not tables added afterward.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the erasure pipeline itself is real, purpose-built, and correctly separated from product soft-delete (unlike a naive deleted_at flag), which is genuinely good design per the research file. The missing piece is purely the verification step: has anyone checked it against every table that now exists.
findings.where_it_should_live: the deferred data-modeling audit (_backend-system/audit/data-modeling.md, not yet created) should include this as its own line item with a table-by-table verdict.
findings.enforcement: checklist: run the data-modeling audit (1b, already scoped and waiting in _plans/BACKEND_LAW.md) with an explicit sub-section cross-referencing every personal-data-holding table against data_deletion_log's actual tables_cleared coverage.
